On the board, “variance of ” is written above the first box with an arrow down to it, and “A constant (bias squared)” is written under the second box. The second form in the outlined box is added here; it is the same statement with the variance written as .

Explanation (added) ✎

This is the same subtract-and-add move as the proof that in Lecture 16: inside the square, subtract and add it back, which changes nothing, then expand. Each line needs a reason on a test:

  1. Line 2. is added inside the bracket, so the value is unchanged.
  2. Line 3. with and . The key fact is that is a number, not a random variable: and are both fixed.
  3. Line 4. The expected value of a sum is the sum of the expected values, and a constant factor comes out: (the rules for from Lecture 8). That is how moves in front of the middle term.
  4. The zero. is a constant and , so . On average, a random variable is at its own mean.
  5. The last line. The first box is the definition of the variance, (Lecture 8), and the variance is . The second box is the expected value of a constant, which is the constant itself: , the bias squared (Lecture 16: bias ).

What it means: the average squared distance from the truth has two separate sources, being off-centre (bias) and being spread out (standard error). In the picture below the bias is 1.2 and the standard deviation is 1, so . For an unbiased estimator the bias is 0 and , which is why smaller variance decides between two unbiased estimators.

Textbook Devore §6.1, p. 251: the mean square error , and the remark that the estimator with the smallest MSE usually cannot be found, which is why the book restricts attention to unbiased estimators. The book never proves the decomposition in the text; it states in Supplementary Exercise 34, p. 274. The standard error is defined on p. 259 (Definition) as .

2Section 7.1 and 7.2: from a point estimate to an interval

Section 7.1 and 7.2   Confidence Intervals

Since is an unbiased estimator with a small standard deviation when is large, if we don’t know the value of , we could draw a simple random sample of size and compute the sample mean . We could then use as a point estimate for .

Although we expect to be close to , it is very unlikely to equal .

Explanation (added) ✎

The sentence combines two facts from the last two lectures. is unbiased, (Lecture 15, and Lecture 16 for the word “unbiased”), and its standard deviation shrinks as grows. So the density of is a tall spike centred on , and one value from one sample lands close to .

“Very unlikely to equal ”: is (approximately) a continuous random variable, and for a continuous random variable the probability of any single value is 0 (Lecture 11). A point estimate will almost always be off by something, and on its own it does not say by how much. The interval in the next section is the fix: it reports the estimate together with a margin.

Textbook Point estimates are §6.1, p. 248 (Definition). Chapter 7 opens (p. 276) with the same point as this board: because of sampling variability it is virtually never the case that , and a single number says nothing about how close it is, so an interval of plausible values is reported instead. Chapter 6 already hints at the idea on p. 260: within about 2 standard errors, .

📘 Raising the confidence level makes the interval wider

The width is

7A question: 100 intervals

Question: If you select 100 independent simple random samples and use them to construct 100 95% confidence intervals, how many of these intervals do you expect will contain ?

No answer is written on the board. “select” is written over another word.

Explanation (added) ✎
Try it first, then open

About 95. Each interval, before its sample is drawn, contains with probability 0.95, and the 100 samples are independent. So the number of intervals that contain is binomial (Lecture 9): , with

You should not expect exactly 95: . Any count from 91 to 99 is ordinary (probability about 0.966 together). About 5 of the intervals miss , and nobody can tell which ones from the data, because is unknown.

This is what “95% confidence” means: it describes the method, how often its intervals catch in the long run. One finished interval either contains or does not.

Based on this sample, the 95% confidence [interval] for is

Question: The manufacturer claims the mean weight of crackers in a box of this type is 36 grams. Do you have a reason to reject the claim?

Yes. We are 95% confident that the value of lies in our 95% confidence interval. Since 36 does not lie in the interval, we have a reason to reject the claim.

The two choices are the same table lookup from either end. In Table A-2, find 0.9750 inside the table: row 1.9, column .06, so . Or find 0.0250: row −1.9, column .06, so . Either gives .

The claim. A 95% interval collects the values of that are reasonable given this sample. 36 is outside, so if really were 36, a sample mean as low as 35.5 would be unusual: it is standard errors below 36, beyond 1.96. That is a reason to doubt the claim, not a proof it is false; the method misses 5% of the time. This is the idea behind the hypothesis tests of §8.1, which start next week after Term Test II.
